title: The invoice inbox nobody mapped
scenario:
You are an operations analyst at a building-supplies wholesaler. The finance team gets about 400 supplier invoices a week by email. The finance director says: "Let's put AI on accounts payable." A vendor has already offered a demo.

Before the demo, you sit with two clerks for a morning and write down what they really do. The exhibit shows your notes.
exhibit:
Accounts payable: notes from one morning (made-up example data)

1. Open the email, save the PDF invoice            ~1 min
2. Type supplier, invoice number, date, total
   into the finance system                          ~4 min
3. Find the matching purchase order, compare
   items and prices                                 ~5 min
4. If prices differ by more than 2%: email the
   buyer and wait for an answer                     1-3 days
5. If the supplier is new: check bank details by
   phone with a known contact                       ~15 min
6. Approve for payment                              ~1 min

Clerk comment: "Step 4 has no written rule. Sometimes we accept a
late fee, sometimes not. Maria just knows."

questions.prompt: The director wants to "put AI on accounts payable". What is the most useful next step?

options.text: Book the vendor demo first, then map the process afterwards based on what the tool can do.
options.explanation: That starts from the tool, not the work. The map is what tells you which demo questions matter.

options.text: Ask the clerks to write the ideal process from the finance handbook, then automate that.
options.explanation: Anthropic's ticket routing guide says to understand how the team handles the work now. The handbook may not show the real steps, such as Maria's unwritten judgment at step 4.

options.text: Judge each step of the map on its own: its input, its output and whether "good" is clear.
options.explanation: Right. "Accounts payable" is too big to judge. Anthropic's support guide says to break the work into tasks so you can prompt and test each one.

options.text: Treat accounts payable as one task and pick the model that scores highest on public tests.
options.explanation: A single big task can't be tested well. The steps have very different inputs, outputs and risks, so they need to be judged one by one.

questions.prompt: Which step is the clearest AI candidate on this map?

options.text: Step 2: read each invoice and fill in supplier, number, date and total.
options.explanation: Right. It has a clear input, a clear output and an easy test: do the fields match the invoice? It also repeats about 400 times a week.

options.text: Step 4: decide whether a price difference is acceptable and reply to the buyer.
options.explanation: The clerk says there is no written rule. If nobody can describe a good decision in one or two sentences, the model can't reliably hit it either.

options.text: Step 5: confirm a new supplier's bank details by calling a known contact.
options.explanation: This is a phone check with a known person. It is a control step, and the notes don't show a written output a model could produce.

options.text: Step 6: approve the invoice for payment once the other steps are finished.
options.explanation: It takes about a minute, and it is the final sign-off on paying money. There is little time to save and a high cost if it goes wrong.

questions.prompt: The director asks why step 4 should stay with a person for now. What is the best reason?

options.text: Models can't read numbers in invoices, so they can't compare prices at all.
options.explanation: Step 3 compares prices too, and the notes don't show a problem there. The issue in step 4 is the missing rule, not reading numbers.

options.text: Step 4 takes 1 to 3 days, so automating it would save too little time to matter.
options.explanation: The days are spent waiting for the buyer. The real blocker is that nobody has written down what a good decision is.

options.text: Any step that needs an email reply should always be handled by a person.
options.explanation: Writing an email is often a good AI task. The blocker here is the unwritten decision rule, not the email.

options.text: The rule is only in Maria's head, so nobody can say what a good decision is.
options.explanation: Right. Write the rule down first, for example "accept differences under 2% if the supplier is on the approved list". Then the step can be tested.
